Each item is once implemented is expected to yield a contribution to the value of the overall product, regardless of the order in which it is implemented. Value may be in the form of new functionality or feature of the product, enhancement to existing functionality, issue fix, or acquired knowledge about the product or processes.

Backlog Items can take numerous forms, some include:

  • User Stories - Explanation of an end user's need for the product, which is typically structured into a short, simple description of the user's needs from their perspective.
  • Features - A capability or functionality of the product that provides value to the end-user. They typically serve as an alternative to documenting requirements in the form of user stories.
  • Epics - A need or requirement that is too big to be estimated and/or is not understood well enough for the team to begin working on it. Epics are typically broken down into individual user stories or features for the team to be able to estimate and work on the item.
  • Themes - A collection of epics, requiring multiple decompositions to reach a level of work that can be estimated and executed.
  • Experiments - Work that is added to the backlog to validate assumptions or otherwise mitigate risks by learning more about either the process, product, or final users.
  • Process Improvements - Typically a result of retrospectives or other means of evaluating team progress and success to date. Process improvements are any actionable items that are added to the backlog to improve the team's processes. This may include changes related to people, processes, tools, etc.
  • Actions to Remove Impediments- Steps that can be taken to unblock the team and allow them to progress in their work. When impediments arise, they are escalated and actionable resolutions are added as a Backlog Item in the Product Backlog, provided their removal requires significant effort from the team.

Backlog items:

  • Should follow the INVEST concept
  • Are the smallest unit of work in that decomposing these items results in smaller Backlog Items
  • Should be short, crisp, and easily understood by all parties from the team responsible for development to the client stakeholders
  • May be refined which may result in a change to either the description or acceptance criteria, thereby requiring a decision as to whether the Backlog Item needs to be re-estimated
  • Exhibit varying levels of granularity and this level of detail evolves over time
    • Backlog Items scheduled for the next sprint tend to be smaller and better understood that those which will be worked on in later sprints
To capture the work that needs to be done, aligned with agile development principles defining what the team needs to deliver.

Without this work product:

  • It is difficult to estimate, plan and track necessary work
  • There is no clear functionality or features to deliver
  • Communication between project stakeholders and developers becomes difficult in terms of conveying the desired functionality or features

All Backlog Items will have a(n):

  • Unique identifier - which can be helpful in maintaining traceability between different Backlog Items
  • Description - of the functionality to be implemented or action to be taken
  • Priority - relative ranking of the importance of the item
  • Effort estimate - expected level of complexity or time to complete, this may be a simple as t-shirt sizing to actual hours
  • Business Value - description or estimate of the value the item will provide to stakeholders once completed

Backlog Items can be documented on/in:

  • Index cards - which can be laid out on a table to facilitate discussing and planning
  • Sticky notes
  • An IT tool, digitally stored and maintained
  • A whiteboard in the team room
